Sporadic trees and power lines were blown down from thunderstorm outflow, from the Friendship Community to Deatsville.
Several trees were blown down on CR-67, east of Moundville, including 3 that fell onto a house.
One person was struck by lightning on Tabor Cut-off Road, near Noccalula Falls.
A few power lines were blown down on Old Sylacauga Highway, by winds estimated around 40 mph.
Trees were blown down at several locations across St. Clair County, including Pell City, Cook Springs, Springville, and Odenville.
Trees were blown down at several locations in the north side of Gadsden, by winds estimated around 45 mph.
A few trees were blown down around Millport and Coosada, by winds estimated around 35 mph.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Kendrick Road and Dogtown Road, and was on the ground for about a half mile.  One chicken house was heavily damaged, two outbuildings suffered minor damage, and several trees were snapped off or uprooted.

A brief tornado touch down was captured on video by several people, near the intersection of CR-27 and CR-69, just west of Winfield.  Subsequent inspection of the touch down area revealed no significant damage.
Several trees were blown down at the intersection of AL-241 and CR-48.
Several trees were blown down on AL-17, near the Detroit Community.
Several trees were blown down in Hamilton, and other locations around Marion County.
Street flooding, up to one and a half feet deep, was reported on AL-118, west of Sulligent.
Straight line winds snapped or uprooted several trees southwest of Berry.  A few of these trees landed on outbuildings producing significant damage.  One mobile home had its roof torn off.

The tornado touched down just west of Jackson Street on the north side of Oakman. It then traveled northeastward, crossed School Street and AL-69, and lifted on Watts Street just east of AL-69. Metal bleachers were twisted and thrown at the Oakman School athletic field, and the concession stand at the ball field was heavily damaged. Oakman Elementary School sustained only light structural damage directly from the tornado.  However, rain leaking through the damaged roof and ceiling caused extensive water damage to parts of the school building. Several houses along AL-69 suffered also significant roof damage. Approximately 150 trees were either uprooted or snapped off.
A few trees were blown down north of Oneonta, and several other locations in the northern part of Blount County.
A few trees were blown down near Hayden.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of US-411, Meyers Road, and Church Road, near the Bethel Baptist Church. It then traveled northeastward and lifted just northeast of AL-174. At least 5 homes suffered extensive roof damage. At least 4 outbuildings were completely destroyed. Approximately 100 trees were either uprooted or snapped off. A glass enclosed sun-room was completely destroyed.
Several streets were closed on downtown Gadsden, due to high water from heavy rain, including Meighan Drive, 4th Street, and Bay Street.
A tree fell onto and damaged a house, near the intersection of I-59 and Noccalula Parkway.
Several trees were blown down on Oakland Drive, near Whorton Bend, south of Gadsden.
Numerous trees were blown down around Troy, and other portions of the county.
Several trees were blown down near Brundidge.
Heavy rain caused water to flow over a bridge on CR-38, east of the Samantha Community.
Heavy rain caused water to flow over a bridge near the Sipsey Community.
Heavy rain caused water to flow over a bridge just north of Hackelburg.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Snow Drive and Old Pineywoods Road, just north of US-78. It then traveled northeastward and crossed CR-77 and lifted shortly thereafter. One mobile home was totally destroyed and rolled approximately 50 feet. At least two additional mobile homes suffered significant damage. Two chicken houses were damaged. A few hundred trees were either snapped off or were uprooted along the path.
Gradient winds blew down several trees around the city of Opelika.  One tree fell onto a house, damaging its kitchen and living room.
Gradient winds blew down numerous trees around Lamar County, including near Sulligent, Vernon, Millport, and Kennedy. At least one of those trees fell onto and damaged a house.
Gradient winds blew down several trees in the western portion of Winston County.
Two and a half to 4 inches of snow fell across the northern and western sections of Marion County.
The tornado briefly touched down near the intersection of AL-69 and Dutton Hill Road.  It damaged 1 carport, 2 sheds, a trailer, and several trees in the area.
Several trees were blown down near the intersection of Empire Road and Hill Road.
Several trees were blown down.

A portion of the roof on a church was torn off, resulting in extensive water damage to the inside of the building. Several ceilings collapsed due to the water damage, and several multimedia equipment items and one electric scooter were also damaged.

Locally dense fog was suspected to be a contributing factor in a boating accident on the Coosa River near the Gadsden Water Works.  One boat ran into a second boat, causing the first to capsize, and the second to become severely damaged.  The five occupants total in the two boats were injured (indirect) in the accident.  Two of the injured were treated and released with minor injuries, while the three others sustained more serious injuries.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Blount County.  Several roads in the city of Oneonta had to be closed due to high water.   A section of CR-30 near Susan Moore was washed out.  Flooding was also reported on Tumlin Drive, southwest of Hayden.  One woman had to be rescued after her vehicle was swept away near Oneonta, and another motorist in the same area was rescued after having their vehicle become encircled by flood waters.  At least two mobile homes were heavily damaged by flood waters.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across the northern half of Tuscaloosa County.  Binion Creek overflowed its banks, causing a section of Old Fayette Road to become closed.  At least a dozen other roads were closed due to flood waters.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Etowah County.  Flood waters helped wash away a culvert and underlying water line northwest of the city of Attalla.  A private dam near the Gallant Community broke, producing up to 12 feet of flooding in the area, and causing about a dozen houses to be evacuated.  Around 12 roads in the county were closed due to flood water.
Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Saint Clair County.  Several roads became impassable due to high water, and had to be closed.
Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Fayette County.  At least one business on Temple Avenue, in the city of Fayette, was damaged due to flood waters.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Cherokee County.  Around a half a dozen roads were closed due to high water.  One car on Park Street, in the city of Centre, was swept away by flood waters, briefly trapping its occupant.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at numerous locations across Lamar County.  Close to 40 roads were closed due to high water, including 10 that were completely washed out.  Just east of Vernon, 3 people were rescued without injury after their car was caught in fast moving flood waters.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Pickens County.  At least 5 roads were closed due to high water, and 2 bridges were washed out.  Flash flooding caused a bridge to wash out on Antioch Chuch Road, over Buncomb Creek.  A mother and child subsequently drove off the washed out roadway, and drowned in the flood waters. A second vehicle following behind also drove into the creek at the same place, but the occupants were successfully rescued.

Heavy rainfall produced flooding at several locations across Walker County.  A bingo hall east of Jasper became flooded, and around 70 people had to be rescued.  Bevill Road near Cordova became flooded, cutting off access to an apartment complex and trapping some of its residents.  Four more people, including a 4 year old boy, were trapped by flood waters on Mitchell Road, south of the Boldo Community.  The child and 2 of the adults were treated for possible hypothermia.  The flood evolved into a river flooding situation, especially on the Mulberry Fork and Warrior River, and took several more days to completely receed.
Heavy rainfall washed out a bridge on CR-347, near the Lynn Community.
A few trees were blown down on CR-11, and CR-334.
Several power lines were blown down on Westover Road.
Several trees were blown down across the county, including around the city of Centre.
Several trees were blown down near Deer Creek Road, and Bulldog Bend Road.

A few dozen large trees were uprooted or snapped along a 1.5 mile long, half mile wide, swath of damage near the city of Oxford.  One mobile home was destroyed when a tree fell on it, and an apartment complex also sustained damage from falling trees.  In all, at least 3 dozen structures sustained varying degrees of damage, most of it roof damage.  Maximum winds were estimated around 85 mph, although most locations experienced winds around 50 mph.
Several trees were blown down near the Perote Community.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees around various parts of Marion County, including the Hamilton, Brilliant, and Guin areas.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees around various parts of Winston County, including the Haleyville and Lynn areas.  A home in Lynn also sustained minor roof damage.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees around and near the city of Vernon.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees around Lake Tuscaloosa.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down trees in several locations around metro Birmingham.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees near Springville.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down several trees near and south of Gadsden.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down trees at several locations around Cherokee County, including near Centre and Spring Garden.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph blew down a tree that fell onto a house, near the Locust Fork community.
Nickel sized hail was reported in the Broomtown community.
Several trees were blown down along AL-35, near Watson.
Reported at exit 153 on Interstate 20.
Reported in the Golden Springs area, east of Anniston.

Winds estimated up to 65 mph produced a roughly half mile radius swath of damage southeast of the city of Anniston.  The most concentrated damage was near the intersection of Greenbrier Dear Road and Birchwood Drive.  Several homes were damaged on Birchwood Drive, mainly due to fallen trees landing on the homes.  A few trees were uprooted and many tree limbs were broken off.  No injuries or fatalities were reported.
Reported on Interstate 20, between mile markers 196 and 199.
Several trees were blown down on Interstate 20, between mile markers 196 and 199.
The tin roof was peeled off a church, and power lines were blown down.
Several trees were blown down along CR-18.
Softball sized hail was reported in the Trickem community.
Several trees were blown down and a barn was damaged near CR-12 and AL-25.
Reported on AL-183, northeast of Uniontown.
Reported on Interstate 20, near the Mercedes plant.
Two homes sustained minor roof damage, several trees were blown down, and one old barn was destroyed, near Vaiden Field Airport.  Winds were estimated around 70 mph.
Reported in the Saks community.
A church was destroyed when winds estimated around 70 mph lifted off its roof and shifted it about 10 feet.  Several trees in the same area were snapped and uprooted.
Penny sized hail covered the ground in the Taylorville community, south of Tuscaloosa.
Power lines were blown down on US-11 near the Fosters community.

The tornado touched down in a forested area one-quarter mile west of County Road 296, about 8 miles northeast of Roanoke. It then tracked east-southeastward for just under a mile before lifting near the Georgia state line. Several hundred trees were either snapped off or blown down along the path, but it hit no other structures.
Reported in the Big Springs community.
Several trees were blown down on Main Avenue and 28th Avenue, in Northport.
A large oak tree was blown down on East Ashby Road.
Power lines were blown down at the intersection of Taylor and Vaughn Roads, in Montgomery.
Winds estimated around 60 mph blew the roof off of both halves of a double wide mobile home, causing it to land 15 feet downwind.  One tree was also snapped off in the same area.
Trees were blown down on AL-171 near Harbin Road.
Trees and power lines were blown down around the Kennedy area.
Penny sized hail was reported at Princeton Hospital in Birmingham.

The tornado touched down briefly near County Road 11 in Chelsea. There was no solid path of destruction, but the tornado was witnessed by several people. Damage in the area included several trees and power lines that were blown down, windows blown out of multiple cars, and a gas station sign that was destroyed.  Winds were estimated around 75 mph.
Several roads around the University of Alabama campus became flooded and temporarily impassable.
Reported near Interstate 65 exit 186.
Multiple 911 calls were received from the public of a tornado crossing AL-69 north of Greensboro.  Only one damaged tree could be found with the apparent brief touchdown.
Old Fayette Road at Brady Montgomery Road became temporarily impassable and was closed due to high water.
Several trees were blown down on CR-19.
Three to six inches of rain caused several roads across Pickens County to become temporarily impassable, including around the city of Reform.
Reported at mile marker 20 on Interstate 20.
Several trees were blown down across roadways in Uniontown.
Several trees were blown down on AL-22, west of Orville.
Baseball sized hail was reported on AL-69 south of US-80.
Several trees were blown down and blocked AL-25, near the Bragg community.
Rainfall of 3 to 6 inches across Lamar County caused as many as 60 county roads to become temporarily closed due to high water.
Reported in the Stokes area, south of Tuscaloosa.

The tornado touched down briefly near the intersection of US-280 and CR-147, near an area known as The Bottle.  One building sustained heavy damage when its metal roof was peeled off. One car was overturned at a used car dealership and a few trees were snapped or uprooted.

The tornado touched down southwest of the community of Salem. It then  moved just north of due east, crossing US-280 and several smaller county roads, before lifting at CR-379.  Winds estimated at 125-130 mph destroyed 6 mobile homes and 4 site built homes, badly damaged 8 homes, and caused minor damage to 9 others.  Two area businesses were destroyed, one other received minor damage, and one school building was damaged.  Hundreds of trees were snapped off and uprooted, and one 18-wheeler was overturned.  There were three minor injuries reported, only one that required hospitalization.

The tornado touched down briefly near CR-51 in far southern Tallapoosa County. Several trees and power lines were blown down and 2 outbuildings were destroyed. A couple of homes in the area also sustained shingle damage.
The snow began around midnight, and accumulated to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 9 am.  Several bridges on future Interstate 22 became snow covered and icy.
The snow began around midnight, and accumulated to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 9 am.
The snow began around midnight, and accumulated to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 10 am.
The snow began just after midnight, and accumulated up to 3.5 inches until it ended around 11 am.
The snow began just after midnight, and accumulated up to 3 inches until it ended around 11 am.
The snow began around 2 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 4 inches until it ended just before noon.
The snow began around 2 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around noon.
The snow began around 230 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around noon.
The snow began around 3 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended just after noon.
The snow began around 3 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 1 pm.
The snow began around 3 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 4 inches until it ended around 130 pm.  The heaviest snow was in the southern portion of the county, near Childersburg and Sylacauga.
The snow began around 3 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 4 inches until it ended around 130 pm.
The snow began around 3 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 4 inches until it ended around 2 pm.
The snow began around 4 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 2 pm.
The snow began around 4 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 3 inches until it ended around 230 pm.
The snow began around 4 am, and accumulated up to 3 to 4 inches until it ended around 330 pm.
The snow began around 6 am, and quickly accumulated up to 3 to 5 inches until it ended around 330 pm.
The snow began around 6 am, and accumulated up to 2 to 4 inches in the northern part of the county, until it ended around 330 pm.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Junkins Road and Holliman Road, in the southeastern portion of Lamar County.  From there, it moved northeastward into Fayette County.  In Lamar County, damage was confined to numerous trees that snapped and uprooted.
Trees were blown down by winds estimated around 50 mph, on CR-9 near the Mission Community.
Several trees were blown down on AL-69, near Blue Water Trace Road.
Several trees were blown down onto power lines, which subsequently caused power outages in the city of Parrish.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Kent Dairy Road and CR-17, near Maylene.  It then moved east-northeast through the old Siluria section of Alabaster, causing sporadic damage, and lifted on the east side of Interstate 65 near exit 238. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted, and three homes were damaged along the path due to falling trees.
Several trees were blown down on Roy Drive, and blocked the roadway.

An 18-wheeler was overturned by winds estimated around 50 mph on Interstate 65 in downtown Birmingham.  Single trees and tree branches were blown down at several locations around the city of Birmingham.
Several trees were blown down in the area around Garmon Road, Whorton Bend Road, and River Cliff Drive.
Trees and power lines were blown down on East Cherry Street.

The tornado that touched down in southeastern Lamar County moved into southwestern Fayette County.  It continued to travel northeastward, across Junkins Drive, Brazeal Road, Wesley Chapel Road, and Howard Drive.  It lifted just north of the intersection of Summers Road and AL-159.  In addition to numerous trees that were snapped and uprooted, the tornado also damaged two homes, one business shop, and at least 5 outbuildings.  A 17 foot camper was pushed 3 feet sideways in the mud due to the force of the wind.  A family that was in one of the homes at the time heard the warning via NOAA Weather Radio and went to their storm cellar.  They then heard the roar of a jet as the tornado passed overhead, but they made it through the event without any injuries.
Two empty chicken houses were damaged near the Teals Crossroads community.
Penny sized hail was reported at a convenience store northwest of Smiths Station.
Penny sized hail was reported at a convenience store northwest of Smiths Station, for the second time in under an hour.
Penny sized hail was reported at a gas station in the Bleeker community.
The roof was blown off a carport on Magnum Road, in the Wellington community.
A tree was blown down and heavily damaged an outbuilding and crushed a vehicle.
An apparent lightning strike caused a tree to fall onto and damage portions of a house, a studio building, a garage, and a car.  Time estimated.

Rain soaked ground led to the failure of an embankment on Morgan Street in Alexander City. The mudslide caused a portion of building to collapse, leaving large holes in the exterior walls of two businesses.  Rain and mud then entered the businesses, heavily damaging or destroying much of the merchandise, and covering the floor with a layer of mud.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.

Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county, including around the cities of Vernon and Sulligent. A mobile home near Vernon sustained significant damage when half of its roof was blown off.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.
Wind gusts estimated up to 50 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county, including the city of Fayette.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.  A tree fell onto an unoccupied truck near Autaugaville.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.  One mobile home near the Coker community sustained damage.
Wind gusts estimated up to 40 mph, associated with an apparent gravity wave, blew down trees at several locations across the county.
Trees and power lines were blown down at several locations around the city of Tuscaloosa.
Single trees were blown down at two locations near Plantersville, in the northern portion of the county.

A large section of the southern portion of Autauga County, from Autaugaville eastward to near Prattville, experienced flash flooding due to several days of excessive rainfall.  Rainfall of 5 to 7 inches over the course of 4 days caused several creeks and small tributaries to the Alabama River to come out of their banks.  The hardest hit area was near Noland Creek, on CR-29 between Autaugaville and Prattville.  Flood waters rose to knee-deep levels in several rooms of a church in that area.  About 10,000 sandbags were placed around the church, and local police officers loaded the church's pews onto a flatbed truck to minimize the damage.
Several trees were blown down near Detroit.
Several trees were blown down on CR-13, near AL-19.  An old store had its walls blown down.
Several trees were blown down in and around the city of Hamilton.
A public official observed a brief tornado touchdown on AL-17, near the Hightogy community.  Subsequent investigation revealed no known damage.
A few trees were blown down on Paul Mills Road, east of the Echola community.
A few trees were blown down on Sawmill Road, west of Lake Tuscaloosa.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Lesueur Road and Old Fayette Road, near the Samantha community. It then moved northeastward for about one half of a mile, and lifted just north of Brady Montgomery Road. The most significant damage occurred as the tornado crossed Brady Montgomery Road. Numerous hardwood and softwood trees were snapped off and uprooted.
Penny sized hail was reported at the intersection of Watermelon Road and Lock 15 Road.
A few trees were blown down near the intersection of Watermelon Road and Lock 15 Road.
Numerous trees and signs were blown down in and around Sulligent.

A large swath of damaging winds, with peak gusts estimated around 80 mph, swept across a large portion of Marion County, from near the Mississippi state line and Lamar County line, eastward to near the Winston County line.  The heaviest damage was in a swath from near the Detroit community, to east of Hamilton.  Hundreds of trees were either snapped off or uprooted. Several of the trees landed on both mobile homes and permanent site homes, as well as several vehicles. Two people in the Byrd community were injured when a tree fell on their mobile home. A restaurant near Guin had its windows blown out and its roof partially removed. A metal billboard structure was bent to the ground, and several other business signs were damaged by the wind. At least one small barn sustained major damage.

Windows were blown out, a ball field dugout, and a baseball batting cage, all sustained damage at Haleyville High School. About 50 students and adults, preparing for the school's prom in the gym, heard about the oncoming storm from a police officer. They took shelter in the basement/locker room area under the gym, and were not injured. Numerous trees and power lines were blown down around the rest of the city of Haleyville. Power lines landed on a vehicle, and briefly trapped its occupants. A tree fell onto a mobile home, slightly injuring one occupant. At least two other homes sustained damage from fallen trees.
Numerous trees were blown down in the city of Fayette.
Several trees were blown down on CR-77 and AL-18, completely blocking the road.
Trees were blown down in the Ashbank community. One of the trees landed on a vehicle, and the occupant suffered a compound fracture.
An 18-wheeler was overturned on future Interstate 22, near Jasper.
One tree was blown down and blocked Alabama Avenue.
A tree was blown down on US-278, and an 18-wheeler then drove into it.  No injuries were reported.
Trees were blown down on Valley Trail, near the Smokerise community.
Trees were blown down onto US-31 near Blount Springs.
Trees were blown down near the intersection of Taylor's Ferry Road and Lock 17 Road, between Sylvan Springs and Oak Grove.
Trees were blown down on Morris-Glenwood Road, near Sam Thomas Road, in Morris.
A large tree was blown down and blocked the road, at CR-55 and US-231, near Blountsville.
Power lines were blown down across Hargrove Road, 63rd Avenue East, and Huntland Drive, between Tuscaloosa and Duncanville.
Power lines were blown down on Wire Road, near Vance.
A tree was blown onto a power pole near the Lake View community.
A large tree fell onto and damaged a home.
Two trees were blown down at the Birmingham Zoo, destroying a bridge, walkway, and light pole.
A few trees were blown down on Pine Hill Road.
Trees and power lines were blown down onto a vehicle on Pine Nountain Road, near Remlap.
Trees were blown down on Mountain View Road, near Springville.
Several trees were blown down, between Pinson and Clay.
Trees were blown down on AL-25 in Vandiver.
Wind gusts were estimated at 60 mph in Maylene.
Trees were blown down on AL-25, near Harpersville.
Several trees were blown down on Lakefront Drive, the Southside community near Gadsden.  At least 4 homes and several vehicles were damaged by falling trees.
Several trees and power lines were blown down near Leota Drive, and on AL-77, near the Southside community.
Trees and power lines were blown down on US-411, near Gaston School.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Lincoln.
In the city of Talladega, a power line was blown down and caused a minor fire, on Hill Street. Trees and power lines were also blown down in several other locations around the city.
A large awning was blown off a service station, and several trees were blown down, in the city of Centre.  Single trees were blown down at several other locations across the county.
A tree was blown down on Overhill Road, and a tree was blown down on Goodwater Highway, in Sylacauga.
A tree was blown down and landed on the roof and deck of a home, in Oxford.
Trees were blown down in Munford.
Trees were blown down on CR-55, in Sterrett.

Thunderstorm winds produced sporadic, isolated, tree damage in several locations of northern Walker County, from near the area around the Walker County Airport, northeastward to the Fall City Road area near the Winston County line. Single trees were reported blown down at each location.
Power lines were blown down in several locations in the city of Anniston.
Trees were blown down at several locations in the city of Ashville.
A metal roof was blown off a residence at US-411 and Loop Road, east of Ashville.
The porch of a house was damaged on Sunset Drive, near Ragland.
Trees and power lines were blown down in Childersburg.
A few trees were blown down north of Selma.
Trees and power lines were blown down on CR-16, near Detroit.
A shopping center in Sulligent suffered roof damage.

A tree was blown down and blocked the roadway, at the intersection of Royal Liberty Road and Settlement Road, near the Royal community.  A vehicle subsequently ran into the tree, but there were no injuries.
A tree was blown down on Broken Arrow Drive.
A barn was blown down on CR-118.
Several trees were blown down in and around the Bear Creek community.

Hail up to the size of golf balls damaged 95 percent of the cars on a car lot on US-280, just south of AL-119.  Damage to most of the cars was slight enough so that they could still be sold at discount, though some received more significant dents.
Trees were blown down on Howells Cove Road.
Reported at Cherokee County High School.
A structure sustained unspecified damage, on US-278 near Snead.
Hail up to penny sized was reported at a gas station near the Strawberry community.  This was the third hail producing storm of the day at that location.
Golf ball to baseball sized hail was reported in and around Cedar Bluff.
Hail up to quarter size was reported at Morgan Creek winery, in Harpersville.
Golf ball sized hail was reported at the EMA office.
Hail ranging from the size of pennies to golf balls fell for several minutes in Ellisville.
Hail up to the size of golf balls fell in the Nixburg community. A few vehicles suffered significant hail damage, and a few homes suffered roof damage from the hail.
Hail up to the size of golf balls fell along AL-63, near the Our Town community. Several windows were broken out and vehicles were damaged.

The tornado started near the intersection of Prospect Road and County Road 45, about 3.5 miles southeast of Martin Dam. It then traveled southeast across AL-49 and several other county and secondary roads, before moving into Lee County. In Tallapoosa County, there were numerous trees snapped off and uprooted along the path. Several outbuildings of various size had their roofs blown off.
Baseball sized hail was reported on AL-63, just northeast of the Kowaliga Bridge.
Hail up to baseball size fell near Martin Dam. The hail was up to 2 feet deep in spots, and was still on the ground the next morning.

The tornado touched down just west of the town of Loachapoka along CR-64. It then moved through Loachapoka, and nearly paralleled AL-14 for several miles, before lifting just south of AL-14 east of CR-51. Hundreds of trees were snapped off and uprooted along the path. In Loachapoka, a church sustained moderate roof damage, several barns and outbuildings suffered varying degrees of damage, and a few vehicles were damaged by the fallen trees.

The tornado touched down south of the Beauregard community, just west of AL-51. It then traveled southeast for just over two miles, lifting near CR-42. The most significant damage occurred near CR-758, where a mobile home received damage, a few other structures suffered roof damage and several trees and power lines were either snapped off or were uprooted.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of CR-83 and Thomas Road. It then traveled east southeast for several miles, crossing US-80 and AL-169 near the Crawford community, before lifting near the intersection of CR-41 and AL-169. The tornado snapped off or uprooted numerous trees along the path.

The tornado touched down near the Phenix City Drag Strip, along CR-28. Most of the damage from the tornado was at a mobile home park, where two minor injuries occurred. A couple dozen trees were snapped and uprooted in the area.
A power line was blown down that caused a brush fire, on Memorial Drive and 6th Street in Prattville.
A power line was blown down on AL-14, on the west side of Autaugaville.
Several trees were blown down and landed on a house, near the intersection of US-80 and Brooks Road, near the Crawford community.

A long tracked tornado, which would eventually track into two other counties, first touched down on Happy Hollow Road just northwest of the Liberty City community, near the Tallapoosa and Macon County line. The tornado was in Tallapoosa County for less than two miles, and caused generally light damage.
Numerous trees were blown down, and 4 to 5 homes were damaged, in Phenix City.

The long tracked tornado that tracked across a large section of Montgomery County made its first of three county line crossings, into Macon County.  In this portion of Macon County, the tornado track was just over a mile long, and through a largely rural area.
Several trees were blown down near CR-2 and CR-6, southeast of Shorter.
Trees were blown down and blocked the road, at the intersection of CR-10 and CR-57, near the Booth community.

The tornado briefly touched down and produced damage near the intersection of Ridge Road and Rutledge Road, about 4 miles east-northeast of Seale. One mobile home was lifted off its foundation, spun and flipped, and completely destroyed. One occupant of the mobile home was injured. Several trees were also blown down along the short path.
Several trees were blown down due to gradient winds ahead of a storm system. Wind gusts were estimated around 45 mph.
Several trees were blown down due to gradient winds ahead of a storm system. Wind gusts were estimated around 45 mph.
A tree was blown down by gradient winds on New County Line Road near Sylacauga.

A tree was blown down by gradient winds and landed on power lines, on Boat Landing Road near Oneonta. A few trees were also blown down in the Locust Fork area. Wind gusts were estimated around 40 mph.

Several trees and power lines were blown down on Jackson Trace Road and Greensport Road, in Ohatchee, due to gradient winds estimated around 45 mph. Trees were also blown down around the cities of Jacksonville and Anniston.
Hail up to the size of pennies covered the ground, near the intersection of Interstates 65 and 459.
The tornado that started in Tallapoosa County crossed into Lee County near Moss Flat Road, before it lifted near Lee Road 217 and Cane Creek. Its brief path in Lee County produced only light damage.

The tornado that touched down near Liberty City in Tallapoosa County crossed into Macon County, and continued to travel southeast, staying just southwest of the Lee County line for most of its path. In Macon County, thousands of trees were either snapped off or uprooted along the damage path. A few mobile homes suffered varying degrees of damage, and one mobile home was knocked off its foundation. Several barns had their roofs partially removed, and several other structures suffered varying degrees of roof damage. Several homes and vehicles had windows broken out.

The tornado that had previously moved through Tallapoosa and Macon Counties completed its journey in Lee County.  It entered Lee County near Lee Road 812 and Long Branch Creek. It traveled another 4.4 miles southeast, before finally lifting near the intersection of US-80 and AL-51, near the Marvyn community.  Most of the path in Lee County was across rural forest or farm land, and damage was relatively minor.
The long tracked Montgomery-Cecil tornado moved out of Macon County, and cut across the far northwestern tip of Bullock County. The track was through a rural part of the county, and damage was light.

After its brief journey across the tip of Bullock County, the Montgomery-Cecil tornado moved back into Macon County, near Bughall Creek.  These last several miles of the path caused damage mainly to trees.  Along the entire path, 3 buildings were destroyed, and another 20 structures suffered varying degrees of damage.  Despite the long path, no injuries were reported.

A long-tracked tornado, that would eventually move into portions of Macon and Bullock Counties, first touched down near the intersection of US-80 (Eastern Blvd.) and AL-110 (Vaughan Road), on the east side of the city of Montgomery. The storm then moved east southeast through the eastern part of the Montgomery metro area, later crossing AL-271 (Taylor Road) and CR-85. It then impacted the Cecil community in the far eastern portion of the county, before moving into Macon County.  At least 3 barns and several outbuildings were damaged or destroyed along the path. Dozens of homes suffered minor to moderate roof damage and numerous windows were broken. Thousands of trees were either snapped off or were uprooted along the path. Several homes and vehicles were damaged from flying or falling debris. An apartment complex on Vaughan Road sustained damage. The most concentrated damage occurred along Ray Thorington Road, where extensive tree damage was apparent, a school was damaged and a few homes were damaged.
Numerous trees were blown down around the county.  Several of the trees landed on homes and vehicles.

Wind gusts estimated around 50 mph blew down numerous trees around the county, including the cities of Vernon and Sulligent.  The wind indirectly caused a two separate vehicle accidents, one with no injuries and with with two injuries (indirect).  Falling trees also caused 3 injuries.  Approximately 8 to 10 homes also sustained damage from fallen trees.

Wind gusts estimated around 50 mph blew down numerous trees around the county.  The roof and press box at Gordo High School were damaged.  Several businesses in Gordo sustained roof damage. A few trees fell on and damaged homes.
Wind gusts estimated around 50 mph blew down numerous trees around the county, including the city of Haleyville.  The roof of a mobile home was damaged in Double Springs.

Wind gusts of 52 mph were measured by a television station's web cam instruments, in Jasper.  Numerous trees were blown down across the county, blocking numerous roadways.  At least 12 homes sustained damage from fallen trees.
Wind gusts estimated around 50 mph blew down numerous trees around the county.  Several of the trees fell onto houses.

Winds gusted to 43 mph at the Birmingham Airport.  A wind gust to 60 mph was measured by sky cam equipment, on top of a high rise building in downtown Birmingham, although surface wind speeds were slightly lower.  Hundreds of trees were blown down countywide, with several of the trees landing on houses.  One tree fell onto a gift shop in Leeds.
Wind gusts estimated around 40 mph blew down numerous trees around the county.
Wind gusts estimated around 40 mph blew down trees in several locations around the county, including Sardis and Selma.  The sign of a business in Selma also sustained damage.

Wind gusts estimated around 40 mph blew down trees in several locations around the county, including the city of Gadsden.  A few fallen trees damaged homes.  The concrete block dugout at a ball field in Glencoe was also damaged.
Wind gusts estimated around 40 mph blew down trees in several locations around the county, including near the city of Prattville.

Winds gusted to 44 mph at the Anniston Airport. Numerous trees were blown down around the county, including the city of Anniston, several of them falling onto homes. A tree fell on an occupied vehicle near Ohatchee, and the driver escaped without injury.  The metal roof of a business in Jacksonville was blown off, and subsequently damaged several cars in a nearby parking lot.
Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down several trees across the county.
Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down several trees across the county.

Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down numerous trees around the county, including the cities of Childersburg, Sylacauga, and Talladega.  At least one tree landed on a home, and another crushed a car.
Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down several trees around the county.
Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down numerous trees around the county.
A wind gust to 43 mph was recorded at the EMA office.  Several trees were blown down across the county, at least one of which landed on a house.

Wind gusts estimated between 50 and 60 mph blew the shingles off of an apartment building in Tuscaloosa.  A wind gust to 58 mph was measured on a television station's web cam instruments.  Numerous trees were blown down around the county.  Several trees fell onto and damaged homes.
Trees and power lines were blown down on CR-391, northwest of Centre.
A tree was blown down onto power lines, just south of the city of Fayette.
A few trees were blown down on AL-14, in the city of Aliceville.
A tree was blown down on Sipsey Valley Road, just north of Kellyton Road.
A tree was blown down on Clements Road, near the Eastern Hills subdivision.
Hail up to the size of golf balls was reported near the Alabama/Mississippi state line, west of the Byrd community.

The tornado touched down just to the west of AL-25 about 1 1/2 miles north of the the town of Whitsitt. It then traveled east-northeast over County Road 47 and lifted just to the east of AL-61, south of the County Road 24 intersection. About 50 trees were snapped or uprooted, and a metal roof was peeled off of an outbuilding.
Hail grew to the size of golf balls in the city of Hamilton.

The tornado touched down on Luke Jackson Road, just east of AL-61.  From there, it traveled to the east-northeast, crossing over several dirt roads before lifting near Webb Road. Along the path, several large hardwood trees were uprooted and snapped, and softwoods were snapped. One home sustained minor shingle damage near the beginning of the path.  A large deer stand was destroyed near the end of the path.

The tornado touched down in Alabaster, near the intersection of US-31 and CR-66. It then traveled northeastward, crossed Interstate 65, and then lifted just after crossing CR-52 near the fire station in Pelham. Numerous trees were snapped and uprooted along the path. A few apartment complexes sustained minor to moderate roof damage. Several fallen trees landed on homes and mobile homes. A large billboard was blown down, which briefly blocked the north bound lanes of I-65.

The tornado touched down in a wooded ravine, between Nichols Lane and CR-7.  It then traveled east-northeast for just over a mile, and lifted near the intersection of Coles Truck Stop Road and AL-5. Along the path, approximately 100 hardwood trees were snapped, and near the end of the path, several hardwoods were uprooted.  A home sustained minor damage to shingles and siding.  The occupant of the home took refuge in a closet, and was unharmed, after her brother called to inform her of the tornado warning.

The tornado a touched down on CR-17, in the the Maylene community.  It then produced sporadic damage as it moved northeastward, crossing Kent Dairy and Thompson Roads, and AL-119, before lifting just before reaching Old Highway 31 and a large shopping center.  Damage along the path was minor, with a few trees being snapped off, and a few homes sustaining light shingle damage.
A few large trees were uprooted along the AL-22 Truck Route, in Maplesville.

The tornado touched down briefly on Mount Lebanon Road, just to the west of the Gibson community in the southern part of Montgomery County.  About 10 trees were snapped or uprooted, the metal roof was blown off a barn, and a home sustained minor shingle damage.

The tornado touched down briefly near the intersection of US-231 and Old Barnes Road, a few miles north of the Pine Level community.  Three horse trailers, including one that weighed over 10,000 pounds, were tossed over 50 feet.
The tornado touched down briefly about two miles north of the Shopton community.  Several trees were snapped or uprooted.

The tornado touched down at the intersection of CR-27 and Jones Chapel Road. It then traveled northeastward and crossed Lake Rd, CR-29, Putman Road, and Hicks Road, before moving into Saint Clair County.  Six chicken houses were completely destroyed, killing nearly 100,000 chickens.  One home had its second story destroyed, and another home suffered a complete roof collapse.  One large industrial barn was destroyed.  Two additional homes, several more chicken sheds, and about 9 outbuilding also received varying degrees of damage.  About 200 trees were snapped and uprooted.

The tornado touched down at the intersection of US-411 and Joshua Drive, several miles northeast of Ashville.  It then moved nearly coincident with US-411 for about 3 miles, lifting just west of Mopar Drive.  About 50 trees were snapped or uprooted, but no other damage was found.
A couple of trees were blown down on CR-71.
A couple of trees were blown down near the intersection of CR-79 and CR-10, near the Creek Stand community.
Several trees were blown down in the city of Talladega.  At least two trees fell onto houses, and another fell onto a car.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of 22nd Avenue and 17th Street in Phenix City.  It then traveled northeast through the south end of Phenix City, and crossed the Chattahoochee River and moved into Muscogee County Georgia.  Five businesses sustained major damage, and seven homes received varying degrees of roof damage.  At least 100 and as many as 200 trees were snapped or uprooted.
Two trees were blown down on the east side of Hamilton.

A brief tornado touchdown was reported by two law enforcement officers in a wooded area near the intersection of AL-18 and AL-107, just northwest of the city of Fayette. A subsequent survey of the area by county officials revealed very little damage.

The tornado touched down along AL-17 just south of the Hightogy Community. It then traveled east-northeast, and lifted after it crossed CR-20 near Wright Road. The damage path was mainly confined to wooded areas. Several trees were snapped off along the path and a few roadways were temporarily impassable.
Several trees were blown down on AL-269, near Parrish.
Several trees were blown down in the Kinterbish Community.

Hundreds of trees were blown down throughout Marengo County, including near Linden. One tractor trailer was blown over on US-80. The driver suffered minor injuries. At least 2 homes in Linden were damaged by fallen trees.
A few trees were blown down along the river, between Forkland and Demopolis.
Several trees were blown down in Cuba.

A brief tornado touched down along CR-10 west of AL-61, which is south southwest of Newbern in the Sunshine Community. The roof and metal siding was completely taken off one barn, and partially off another.  Another cinder block building on the farm sustained roof damage. A few trees were blown down along the short path.

Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across Hale County, including around Greensboro. A total of 9 homes were damaged by fallen trees, including 5 homes in the Faunsdale area. One mobile home had its roof torn off.

The tornado touched down near Ashington Drive, in the Brook Highland area, just southwest of Lake Purdy.  It then moved east-northeast, across AL-119, and into the Greystone area.  Numerous trees were uprooted along the path. At least 20 homes suffered minor roof damage, mainly the loss of shingles. Other damage was limited to uprooted and snapped trees, especially on the Greystone golf course. The course was closed for a day due to clean up.
Thousands of trees were blown down across Perry County.
Trees were blown down on Stevens Hill Circle, Riverchase Trace, and Old Rocky Ridge Road, in Hoover.  Large tents and portable restrooms were blown down at Spain Park.

The tornado touched down along CR-470 west of Dunavant.  It then moved northeastward, and lifted just after it crossed AL-25 just north of Dunavant. Numerous trees were snapped off and uprooted along the path.
Hail up to the size of nickels covered the ground at Greystone Legacy Country Club.
Numerous trees were blown down across the southern portion of Bibb County, and many roadways were blocked as a result.

A brief tornado touched down near the intersection of Sequoyah Road and Cherokee Road, near the Stewarts Crossroads Community. Several trees were blown down along the short path. At least 10 homes suffered minor to moderate damage associated with the fallen trees.
Several trees were blown down at several locations around the city of Moody.
Hail up to the size of quarters covered the ground in Vandiver.

Trees and power lines were blown down around Maplesville. At least three homes and two mobile homes were damaged by the fallen trees. Fallen trees blocked the railroad tracks. Several outbuildings suffered varying degrees of roof damage.
Hail up to the size of nickels covered the ground, near Sterrett.

The tornado touched down in Pleasant Grove along CR-27. It then tracked northeastward and generally paralleled CR-27 and Wolf Creek. The tornado crossed Interstate 20 near the intersection of US-231 in Pell City, and continued northeastward all the way to the Coosa River just beyond the River Ranch Road Community. Numerous trees and power poles were snapped off along the path. Many fallen trees and power poles landed on homes and outbuildings.
Several trees were blown down in the city of Clanton.  At least one home was damaged by fallen trees.

Several trees were snapped off along Interstate 65, between mile markers 219 and 212, and several more were blown down within the city of Jemison. An old store front was blown over in downtown Jemison. Four buildings suffered damage. At least 3 vehicles were damaged by fallen trees. The railroad tracks were blocked for several hours. The fence around the baseball field at Jemison High School was blown down.
A large tree was blown down in the city of Thorsby.

Hundreds of trees were snapped off at CR-71 and South River Road, near Lacoosa Marina. At least 3 homes were damaged by the fallen trees. Several campers also suffered minor damage. A roof was blown off a dry storage boat house, and several other outbuildings were damaged.
Several trees were blown down in the Benton Community.
Several trees were blown down across Autauga County.
Several trees were blown down in the northwest portion of Coosa County.
Numerous trees were blown down across Lowndes County. Many of the fallen trees blocked roadways. A few trees fell on vehicles and homes.
Several trees were blown down in the Eden Community, near Pell City.
Several trees were blown down in Columbiana.
Numerous trees were blown down and uprooted around Sylacauga. The volunteer fire department suffered roof damage. A few homes and mobile homes were damaged by the fallen trees.
Several trees were blown down on Old Sylacauga Highway and Odens Mill Road, north of Sylacauga.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Elmore.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Millbrook. Some of the fallen trees blocked roads, and one tree fell onto a home causing minor damage.
Trees and power lines were blown down in several locations around Elmore County, including Wetumpka. A few vehicles were damaged by the fallen trees.
Several trees were blown down near Lakeview Drive, on the northeast side of Montgomery.
A large tree was blown down on Woodley Circle, on the southeast side of Montgomery.
The soccer field bleachers at the Auburn University at Montgomery were blown over.
Several trees were blown down across Clay County. At least one structure suffered unspecified wind damage.
Power lines were blown down on Cricket Lane, in Lincoln.
A small portable metal shed was destroyed and blown across US-278 into the parking lot of a nearby gas station. A few trees were blown down, and a few homes suffered shingle damage.
Trees were blown down at several locations around Tallapoosa County, at least one of which landed on and badly damaged a house.
Trees were blown down at several locations across Macon County. At least one home was damaged by the fallen trees. At least one vehicle was damaged, and many roadways were blocked.

Trees and power lines were blown down at several locations across Lee County. A church roof sustained moderate damage, and a parking deck had minor roof damage. A large tree fell onto a county bucket truck, and damaged the county garage shop.
The East Alabama Medical Center recorded a peak wind gust of 61 mph.
Trees were blown down at several locations around Chambers County. A few vehicles were damaged by the fallen trees.
Several trees were blown down and caused power outages. The fallen trees damaged several buildings and vehicles. Several outbuildings and barns also suffered damage.
Several trees were blown down on US-278 in Hamilton.
An estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain caused US-278 in Sulligent to become impassable due to flooding.
Several trees were blown down west of the Moreland Community.

The tornado touched down along the Tombigbee River basin near the Rogersville Camp area. It then tracked northeastward for about a mile before it lifted. Several trees were snapped off and several tops of trees were taken off along the path. Some of the fallen trees landed on trailers and caused varying degrees of damage.

The tornado touched down in Carrollton near the intersection of Rose Street and CR-35. It then tracked east-northeast and lifted in a rural area along Lubbub Creek. Several trees were snapped off or were blown down along the path. A few of the trees fell on homes and caused varying degrees of damage.

The tornado touched down briefly near AL-13, south of the New Lexington Community.  Two homes sustained moderate damage. One home had its garage door blown in and subsequently a wall blown out. Wind entered into another home's attic and blew out a portion of the roof. A wooden projectile (1 by 6) was blown approximately 100 yards and embedded into the side of a home. A pontoon boat was also overturned.

The tornado touched down along CR-21 on the western side of Lake Arnedra, crossed the lake, and then lifted on the eastern shore.  Two large hardwood trees were blown down onto houses causing major damage to one of the homes and making it uninhabitable. Another hardwood was toppled on the western shore of the lake.
Several trees were blown down near Panola.
A mobile home was damaged by thunderstorm winds in the Fosters Community.
Storm spotters reported trees down and roof damage to a building.
Several trees were uprooted on Mitchell Mountain Road, near the Corona Community.

The tornado touched down near the eastern city limits of Jasper, tracked eastward across Highway 78, and lifted near Golf Course Road. Five structures were damaged.  A bank drive through structure was detached from the main building and rotated 90 degrees.  Two car dealerships sustained damage.  Forty cars were totaled, mostly due to broken windows resulting in water damage.  Three air handlers atop the dealerships were rolled. Numerous trees were uprooted. A billboard was also impaled by a fiberglass missile.

The tornado touched down on the west side of Cordova along South Street. It then moved east-northeastward through the city of Cordova, and lifted shortly after it crossed near the intersection of Disney Street and Mass Avenue, near Cane Creek. Numerous trees were snapped off or were uprooted along the path. At least 15 homes were damaged by the fallen trees. One of the trees fell on a train and damaged some of the cars but the train did not derail.
At least two vehicles were flipped on future I-22, near the Cordova/Parrish exit.

A tornado briefly touched down along Highway 69 and crossed the road before lifting. A carport was destroyed with debris scattered across the road. Several trees were uprooted and snapped and a trampoline was carried 200 yards downwind. A utility pole was also snapped but was likely impacted by debris.
The tornado briefly touched down along CR-5, approximately 2 miles west of Interstate 65. The tornado uprooted several trees in a relatively small concentrated area.
Several trees were blown down on AL-79, near Cleveland.

Widespread wind damage was reported across the Birmingham metro area. Trees and power lines were blown down in numerous locations, and several homes were damaged by the fallen trees. Locations that reported damage included Irondale, Bessemer, Hoover, Birmingham, Pinson, Vestavia Hills, Warrior, Corner, and Fairfield.
A tree was blown down on US-231 near Oneonta.
Trees were blown down between Ohatchee and Alexandria.
Hail up to the size of nickels was reported at the WAKA-TV studio.

The tornado briefly touched down in the Albritton Road and Sparks Drive area near Warrior. Several large hardwood trees were uprooted, and several pines were snapped. Some of the trees fell onto and caused damage to houses. Several other homes in the area lost roof shingles.
Flash flooding caused numerous roads to become impassable.  High water was reported on several county roads, in and around the city of Union Springs.

Numerous county roads and city streets became impassable and suffered extensive damage due to flooding caused by torrential rainfall.  The cities of Wetumpka, Millbrook, and Deatsville were especially hard hit. At least 43 homes, 10 business, and 2 churches also suffered damage due to the flooding. The Millbrook city parks and recreation areas suffered substantial damage.

Numerous county roads and city streets became impassable and suffered extensive damage due to flooding caused by torrential rainfall. The city of Prattville was the hardest hit area, as the storm water drainage system was extensively damaged. At least 32 homes and 6 business also suffered damage due to the flooding. Several residents of a mobile home community had to be evacuated when flood waters threatened their homes.

The city of Montgomery experienced extensive flash flooding due to a period of very heavy rainfall. An estimated 10+ inches of rain fell in portions of Montgomery County in about a six hour time frame. The downtown area, including the capitol district, was hit especially hard.  At least three feet of water flowed into the basement of the Statehouse building, and state legislators temporarily moved to backup chambers in the old Capitol. Numerous streets downtown were closed, and numerous cars became stranded in the high water. One 67 year old man drowned when his car was swept away by flood waters in Montgomery.
Flash flooding caused numerous roads to become impassable.  High water was reported on several city and county roads, in and around the city of Tuskegee.
Two trees were blown down onto power lines and a car, on Renfroe Road east of the city of Talladega.
A lightning strike caused a house fire, on Lee County Road 390.
Nine trees were blown down on Interstate-85, between mile markers 70 and 74.
Several trees were blown down on Lee County Road 266.
Several trees were uprooted and snapped off, on CR-271 near Valley.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Fairfax.

Several roads in and near the city of Roanoke were closed due to flash flooding.  These roads included Chestnut Road, Louina Road, and CR-45 near Rockstand Road.  County Road 41, near the Corinth Community, had four feet of water rushing across it.

The weak tornado touched down briefly just south of CR-20 and traveled to the northwest for about a third of a mile before it lifted. Damage along the path included 4 hardwood trees uprooted and 1 softwood tree snapped, and minor roof damage to an outbuilding.

The weak tornado touched down in northeast Lee County on the south side of Halawaka Creek. Starting just to the west of Forest Road and traveling to the northwest, the tornado lifted after it crossed Lee Road 462 and crossed into the lake. Damage along the path included approximately 150 trees snapped or uprooted, several of which fell onto homes and other buildings, including sheds and boat houses.
A tree was blown down and fell onto a power line, in Arley.
Several trees were blown down in Double Springs.
The intersection of CR-20 and AL-39 was washed out due to heavy rainfall.
Several trees were blown down on US-82, near Duncanville.
Several trees were blown down on Cold Springs Road, in Cottondale.
A portion of a large billboard was blown down on I-20, exit 77, which struck a vehicle.
One tree was blown down, blocking CR-28.
Reported on the Auburn University campus.
Power lines were blown down at CR-68 and CR-139.
Several trees were blown down on Camp Parkman Road, southwest of Phenix City. At least two homes were damaged by the fallen trees.
Heavy rainfall caused street flooding on Opelika Road, east of Gay Street, in Auburn.
Heavy rainfall caused street flooding on AL-63, north of Alexander City.
Eight inches of running water was reported over CR-49, in Beaverton.
Two feet of running water was reported over AL-18 West, one foot of running water was reported over AL-17, and eighteen inches of water was reported over CR-9, all in the city of Vernon.
Several trees were blown down on CR-41, north of Addison, and subsequently damaged a fence.
Several trees were blown down in the Sardis City community.
Several trees were blown down in Munford.
Numerous trees were blown down in the southeastern portion of Lamar County, mainly east of AL-17.
Several trees were blown down on AL-18, near the Crossville community.
Several trees were blown down onto a house, in the Belk community, briefly trapping people inside.
A few trees were blown down in northern Tuscaloosa County, near Samantha.
A tree fell onto a power line, south of Abernant.
A few trees were blown down near the Ethelsville community.
Several trees were blown down onto AL-140, just east of Echola Road.
A tree was blown down onto Lawson Gap Road, near the Mountainboro community.
A few trees were blown down in the southwestern portion of Marion County.
Several trees were blown down on US-278, near Sulligent.
Several trees and power poles were knocked down near and north of Hackleburg.
Several trees were blown down and blocked the road, near Musgrove Chapel.
Several trees were blown down and blocked AL-18, about a mile south of Vernon.
Several trees were blown down in the Whitehouse community, in eastern Marion County.
A tree was blown down on Fairview Road, in Winfield.
Numerous trees were blown down across the width of Fayette County, from the Belk community and city of Fayette in the west, to the city of Berry and Boley Springs community in the east.
The metal roof was blown off a building, on CR-114 northwest of Haleyville.
Numerous trees were blown down across Lamar County, starting near Detroit in the north, continuing through the city of Vernon, all the way to Kennedy in the south.
Several trees were blown down in the southern portion of Alexander City.
Several roads in the downtown area of Vernon became temporarily impassable due to flooding.
Several trees were blown down near Hackleburg, temporarily blocking several roads.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across a large portion of Winston County, from Haleyville in the west to Arley in the east.  Winds in Haleyville were estimated around 65 mph.
An estimated 25 to 30 trees were blown down at the Musgrove Country Club, in the Manchester Community.
Winds were estimated around 60 mph in the Corner community.
Several trees were blown down, near Pleasant Grove.
A few trees were blown down near the Hayden community.  One tree landed on a vehicle.
A few trees were blown down and blocked the road, in the Shady Grove community.
Several trees were blown down on Warrior River Road, and Garywood Road, in Hueytown.
Several trees were blown down near CR-52 and CR-13, in Helena.

Wind gusts were estimated between 50 and 70 mph in downtown Birmingham.  Trees were blown down in numerous locations around the city.  A tree fell onto a home in Vestavia Hills, causing substantial damage.
Winds were estimated up to 60 mph in the Inverness area of northern Shelby County.  A television station skycam, about 50 feet up on top of a hotel building, measured a wind gust of 74 mph.
Power lines were blown down on US-31, in Pelham.
A single tree was blown down on Old Acton Road, north of Moody.
A tree was blown onto a house on Blackjack Road, near Argo.
A few trees and large branches were blown down in and around the city of Eutaw.
Wind gusts over 60 mph were estimated at the Chula Vista exit on Interstate 20.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Pell City.
A few power lines were blown down in the city of Gadsden.
Several trees were blown down and completely blocked the road, near the intersection of CR-51 and Shallow Creek Road, near Westover.
Several trees and power lines were blown down around the city of Childersburg.
Several power lines were blown down near the Stemley community.
Trees were blown down and blocked South Main Avenue, in the city of Sylacauga. A tree fell onto a moving vehicle, but no one was injured.
Several trees were blown down in Lincoln. The glass was blown out of a window of a mobile home, injuring the occupant.
Several trees and power lines were blown down across CR-55, west of Wilsonville.
Several trees were blown down at the intersection of AL-145 and Pinedale Road, near Clanton.
A large tree was blown down and blocked 4 lanes of traffic, on AL-22 in the New Site community.
Several trees were blown down on Mines Road, west of Ashland.  Trees were also blown down on State Lake Road, and Church Road.
Remnant outflow winds of diminishing thunderstorms blew down a tree and blocked CR-329, near the Fosters Crossroads community.
A car became trapped between two trees that were blown down onto CR-40 and CR-19, near the Independence community.  Wind were estimated around 50 mph.
A tree fell across and blocked CR-63, in the New Hope Community.
A large tree was blown down on CR-58, near the Booth community.
Remnant outflow winds from diminished thunderstorms blew down several trees around the city of Oxford.  Winds were estimated around 45 mph.
Trees and power lines were blown down at several locations in the western portion of Marion County.
A few trees were blown down near the Detroit community.
A few trees were blown down near the Henson Springs community.
Trees and power lines were blown down around the city of Guin.
Trees were blown down along US-278, near the Natural Bridge community.
A couple of trees were blown down in the city of Double Springs.
A single tree was blown down across AL-18, just west of the city of Fayette.
Trees and power lines were blown down across AL-13, near the Delmar community.

Numerous trees were blown down in a swath across the middle of Walker County, from the Blackwater and Macedonia communities, eastward to AL-157.  Fallen trees damaged at least one home, one mobile home, and one camper.
A few trees were blown down near the Boldo community.
Trees and power lines were blown down on Billy Bingham Road, and CR-38, near the Samantha community.
Trees were blown down along AL-79, between Locust Fork and County Line.
Trees were blown down on Tierce Patton Road, near Beacon Point Drive, near Lake Tuscaloosa.
A few trees were blown down on AL-79, east of Blountsville.
Trees were blown down and blocked AL-160, near the Hayden community.
A single large tree was uprooted on 3rd Avenue, in Pleasant Grove.
A single tree was blown down on CR-59 and Hatton Creek Bridge.
A few trees were blown down and blocked the roadway, on Virginia Drive in Hueytown.
Trees and power lines were blown down at Ensley Avenue and Avenue W, in Ensley.
A single large tree was blown down and blocked Covered Bridge Road, north of the Coaling community.
A few trees were blown down and blocked Cimmaron Drive, in Bessemer.
Winds were estimated around 65 mph near Rocky Ridge Road and Wisteria Drive.
Trees were blown down on Pine Grove Road, and in the Berry Mountain area, near the Rosa community, northwest of Oneonta.
Street flooding caused a portion of 3rd Avenue and 4th Street to become temporarily impassable.
Several trees were blown down in the northern and western part of Saint Clair County, including near Odenville.
Several roads were flooded in Pelham, and were temporarily impassable.
Trees were blown down on Oak Ridge Drive, in Pelham.
Trees were blown down on CR-36, about a mile from CR-11, west of Chelsea.
Trees and power lines were blown down at the Oneonta Library.
Trees and power lines were blown down at Caldwell Mill and Camp Horner Roads.
Peavine Road, in Oak Mountain State Park, was temporarily closed due to downed trees blocking the roadway.
The old National Standard building in Columbiana, which had been vacant for several years, suffered a collapsed roof.
Power lines were blown down at the intersection of AL-145 and CR-42, east of the town of Shelby.
Several large tree limbs were broken off, in Childersburg.
A single tree was blown down and blocked Crest Drive, in the city of Talladega.
A tree was blown down on Interstate 20, mile marker 175, blocking one lane.
A few trees and power lines were blown down around the Marbury area, some of which blocked roadways.
Power lines were blown down AL-9, near Ashland.
A few trees were blown down in Billingsley, including a few that blocked roads.
Trees were blown down at several locations in and around the city of Lineville.
Several trees were blown down onto US-31, just south of the Chilton/Autauga County line.
Trees were blown down on AL-22 east of Alexander City.
A few trees were blown down near the Independence community.  One fallen tree blocked the road, and another tree fell onto a mobile home.
Several trees were blown down around the city of Wetumpka.
A large tree was blown down and blocked Airport Road, near the Coosada community.
Trees were blown down at several locations around the city of Prattville.
At least two homes were damaged by fallen trees, in the Stillwaters community along Lake Martin.

Numerous trees were blown down across Elmore County, including the communities of Redland, Santuck, Emerald Mountain, Friendship, Red Hill, and Weldon Road, and the cities of Wetumpka and Tallassee.  A tree fell onto a barn in Tallassee.
Two trees were blown down onto CR-15, on the east side of the river bridge, near the Malone community.
An outbuilding of a house was destroyed at the intersection of AL-120 and AL-49, in Reeltown.  Some shingles were blown off the roof of Reeltown High School.
Trees and power lines were blown down at several locations around the city of Montgomery, both in and just outisde the city limits.
Numerous trees were blown down on East University Drive and Shelton Mills Road, near Auburn University.
Large trees were blown down on Lee Road 17, south of Auburn.
Trees were blown down on US-29, near the Banks community.
Trees were blown down on Summerville Road, in Phenix City.
Trees and power lines were blown down at several locations around the city of Eufaula.
A few trees were blown down on future Interstate 22, about 3 miles east of the Mississippi state line.
A few trees and power lines were blown down, near the Summit community.
Several trees were blown down on US-278, near Snead.
Trees and power lines were blown down on AL-79, near the Locust Fork community.
A mobile home was blown off its foundation, in the Wynville community.  Two occupants were briefly trapped and sustained unspecified injuries.
Large trees were blown down on Pacota Drive in Oneonta.
Trees and power lines were blown down on US-31, near the Blount Springs community.
A few trees were blown down on West Hill Road, in Palmerdale.
Several trees were blown down in and around Detroit, completely blocking AL-17.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in Altoona.  Some of the trees landed on homes and cars.
Trees and power lines were blown down at Cove Road and Rock Crusher Road, near the Whitney Junction community.
Trees were blown down on US-11 and Terry Street, in the city of Springville.
Trees were blown down onto I-59, at mile marker 174.
A few trees were blown down on Moores Street, in Steele.
Chandler Mountain Road, west of Steele, had to be completely closed due to multiple trees that were blown down across it.
Winds estimated at 60 mph were observed on Mary Taylor Road, in Trussville.
Trees were blown down at several locations around the city of Gadsden.
Several trees were blown down in the western portion of Calhoun County, near Ohatchee.
At least three trees were blown down on Wolf Pond Road, north of the Renfroe community.  One of the trees landed on a vehicle.
A large tree and power lines were blown on Battle Street and Martin Luther King Jr. Drive, in the city of Talladega.
Trees were blown down and blocked the road, at the intersection of Patricia Avenue and Glenwood Drive, in the city of Talladega.
A few trees were blown down around the city of Anniston.  A large tree limb fell onto a home, destroying a porch and damaging the adjoining roof.
Trees were blown down and blocked US-280, between Harpersville and Childersburg.
Trees were blown down and blocked Oldfield Road, in the Sycamore community.

Trees were blown down at several locations in Alexander City.

Several trees were blown down around Dadeville.
Several trees were blown down in far southern Tallapoosa County, near Lake Martin.
Golf ball sized hail damaged the windshields of some cars, on US-280 between Harpersville and Childersburg.
Trees were blown down south of Tallassee.
Power lines were blown down on Lake Street in the city of Auburn.
Trees were blown down onto power lines in the city of Opelika.
Trees were blown at several locations around the city of Gadsden.
Numerous trees and power lines were blown down across Calhoun County, from near Ohatchee and Alexandria, southward through Saks and into the city of Anniston.
Trees were blown down in the Pine Tuckey community.
Several trees and power lines were blown down on CR-27, near Millport.
One or two trees were blown down on AL-69, near the Windham Springs community.
Several trees were blown down in Camp Hill.
Several power lines were blown down in the city of Opelika.
One tree landed on a power line, just west of Blountsville.
A large metal sign was blown down onto a restaurant building, and the metal roofing was peeled off an office building, in the city of Montgomery.
Large limbs were broken off a tree, and lawn furniture was blown about 100 feet.
Trees and power lines were blown down near the intersection of CR-72 and CR-73.
A large aluminum shed was blown onto Interstate 65, near mile marker 169, on the west side of Montgomery.
Trees were blown down on Pine Ridge Trail, near Phenix City.
Trees were blown down on Buyck Road, between the Titus and Buyck communities.
Trees were blown down at several locations around the city of Clayton.
A large sign for a restaurant and motel was blown down onto a road, briely blocking it.

A lightning strike at the Alabama Department of Transportation office in Talladega caused considerable damage, both to the outdoor grounds and to equipment on the inside.  The lightning apparently struck a flag pole in front of the building, and then ran down the pole into the ground.  The underground current created a small ditch and blew out a portion of a concrete sidewalk.  From there it continued into the building, burning down an awning, blowing out a window, and ultimately frying several pieces of computer equipment.  Damage to the grounds was estimated around $2000 to $3000 dollars, with the computer equipment between $10,000 and $20,000.
Trees were blown down in several locations around the city of Troy.
A tree fell onto a house in the Spring Hill community.
Several trees were blown down on Old Highway 18, east of Vernon.
Several trees were blown down on Moscow Road, near Sulligent.
A female was struck by lightning on Bouldin Dam Road.
Large trees were blown down and blocked CR-40.  A power line was snapped in half, and a high voltage transformer was on the ground.
A tree was blown down across Main Street, in the city of Millbrook near the post office.
A few trees were blown down at Pierce Chapel Road and AL-9, in the Santuck community.
Wind gusts estimated at 60 mph were reported about 2 miles northwest of the Red Hill community.
