One tree was blown down onto power lines near Liberty Park.
Power lines were blown down in Addison.
Trees were blown down on AL-13, just north of US-278.
A single large tree was blown down on Settlement Road, in Sylacauga.
A single tree was blown down and briefly blocked a lane of Interstate 65, near exit 287.
Unspecified roof damage occurred to a couple of homes on the east side of the city of Tallassee.
Winds damaged a sign on Interstate 65, near exit 179.

At least 10 trees were blown down around the city of Selma, including a few that fell onto homes and caused significant damage.  At least one of the homes' occupants was briefly trapped, but was otherwise uninjured.
Winds estimated around 50 mph blew down trees on CR-146, southeast of Auburn.
Winds estimated around 45 mph blew a tree down onto a power line, west of Selma.
Winds estimated up to 50 mph blew down isolated trees and tree limbs at several locations around the city of Tuscaloosa.  One tree blocked a roadway, and another landed on a vehicle.
Winds estimated around 50 mph peeled some tin roofing off a building.
A few trees were blown down near the Glen Allen community.
Power lines and at least two trees were blown down, near the intersection of AL-171 and Camp Comfort Road.
Winds estimated around 45 mph blew a tree down onto a power line, near Arley.
Winds were estimated around 70 mph in the town of Addison.
Several trees were blown down in the Detroit community.
Heavy rains caused water to overflow several streets in the Ensley area.  A vehicle became stranded in flood waters, near the intersection of 18th Street and Avenue V.

At least 20 trees were blown down across various parts of Etowah County, mainly around the city of Gadsden.  Fallen trees struck two homes in the 1400 block of 4th Avenue in the city, and another tree struck a house on 4th Street.
A pine tree was blown down and partially blocked AL-17, near CR-9, south of York.
Several trees and power lines were blown down, causing damage to the roof of at least one home.
A large tree was blown down onto AL-14, west of Wetumpka.  Two vehicles subsequently ran into the fallen tree, although the occupants were not injured.
Trees were blown down onto the northbound lanes of US-231, near Jasmine Hill Road in Wetumpka.
Winds estimated at 40 mph blew down power lines at the intersection of Lee Road 294 and Lee Road 430, in the Smiths Station community.
Trees were blown down at several locations near the city of Wetumpka.  One large tree brought down power lines and poles, which blocked a portion of Willow Springs Road.
Heavy rains caused water to flow over AL-119, near Briarwood Christian School.
Heavy rain caused water to cover the road, which led to the closure of AL-160 at Locust Fork.
Six inches of water was reported to be flowing across CR-49, near Kennedy.
Six inches of water was flowing across 5th Street, near Main Avenue, in Northport.
Up to six inches of water was flowing across Walker Chapel Road, in Fultondale.
Heavy rains caused water to flow over a bridge, on Hunter Creek Road, just south of McFarland Boulevard.
Winds estimated around 45 mph blew down a tree on 42nd Street, in Ensley.
Six inches of water was flowing across S.A. Graham Boulevard, in Brundidge.
Water was reported flowing over Elba Highway, just north of the Spring Hill community.
Winds estimated around 45 mph blew a single large tree down onto a house, north of the Mount Olive community.

Lightning struck and damaged an apartment building in the Rainbow City area, near Gadsden, which caused heavy smoke outside the building.  Two units of the building had to be evacuated, as firefighters searched for the source of the smoke.  The time of the event is estimated.
A portion of CR-115, near the Safford community, was washed out do to heavy rainfall.
A lightning strike caused a house to catch fire, on CR-82 near the Hawk community, resulting in unspecified damages.
A pole barn/storage shed was damaged and a couple of trees were blown down by winds estimated around 45 mph, between the Addison and Grayson communities.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Reed Road and Judge Avenue, where it removed a few shingles off of a home and peeled back the tin roof of an outbuilding. It continued north-northeastward across Old Henry Road, to the intersection of US-31 and Lomax Drive.  Eyewitnesses at this location photographed the tornado as it moved away.  A metal roof was totally lifted off of an outbuilding, with portions of this debris deposited nearly a half mile downstream.  Damage was|relatively minor and limited to a very narrow yet discernible path.  Peak winds were estimated between 60 and 70 mph.
At least one road in downtown Montgomery had to be closed due to flooding.
Winds estimated around 40 mph blew down isolated trees on Tuskegee Circle, and Forrest Road, in the city of Gadsden.
A car became stalled due to high water near Posey Field Airport near Haleyville, and water was flowing over CR-11, about a mile east of the Airport.
Flooding described as major was reported on Ben Martin Drive, west of the Wellington community.  The underpinning was removed from several mobile homes in the area.
About a foot of water was flowing over First Avenue West, near the Alabaster Public Library.
Flood waters entered several homes in the Hillsboro Lane and Rocky Ridge Drive areas of Helena.
One person was trapped in a home by flood waters, at the 1500 block pf Pratt Highway in Forestdale.
Several water rescues were made around the Birmingham Metro area due to the flooding, including a woman that was trapped in her vehicle by flood waters along Village Creek.
Flooding was reported on Main Street, near the Post Office, in Margaret.
Flooding was reported in portions of Odenville.  A car on Foreman Drive began to float in the flood waters.

Water was flowing over the road at the intersection of CR-52 and CR-17 in Helena.  At least a dozen vehicles became trapped and roads had to be closed at Joe Tucker Park, due to flood waters flowing over the spillway there.
Flooding, described as major, was reported in Argo, with almost a foot of water into some businesses on Main Street.
Many streets in the city of Leeds had to be closed due to flooding.  Several cars became stranded in the flood waters.
At least six inches of flowing water was reported in the Willow Brook Trailer Park.
All four lanes of US-278, east of Sulligent, had to be closed due to water flowing over them.
Several streets in the city of Fayette, including the intersection of US-43 and AL-18, became impassable due to flooding.
Numerous roads in the city of Jasper were covered with water and became temporarily impassable.
Several roads around the city of Deatsville had to be closed due to high water.
More than 40 cars of a train derailed near the Mortar Creek crossing, due to a portion of the tracks being washed out from heavy rain.  A portion of CR-64 neaby was also washed out.
Martin Road, and Red Barn Road, both had to closed due to water running over the roads.
Several county roads around Coosa County had to be closed due to water over them, including CR-119, CR-16, CR-112, and CR-37.
A portion of AL-49 became temporarily impassable, due to high water.
A portion of CR-7 near the Brownsville community became temporarily impassable due to high water.

A portion of the Little Cahaba River backed up due to not being able to flow into the swollen main channel of the Cahaba River, which had risen due to rainfall during the overnight hours.  The overflow of the Little Cahaba caused the closure of Bailey Road in the city of Leeds, where the water reached a depth of at least 4 feet.
Several roads around Camp Hill, including AL-50 and CR-89, had to be closed due to high water making them temporarily impassable.
The intersection of Mill Street and Maple Street, in the city of Brent, became temporarily impassable due to high water.
Overflow of Oakmulgee Creek caused road closures near the intersection of AL-219 and CR-64, east of the Sprott community.
Water was flowing over the road at the intersection of US-280 and Lee Road 175, near the Salem community.
Water was flowing across the roadway in the Cusseta community.
Water was flowing over the bridge at Opelika Road and Cutrate Road, in Phenix City.
Union Hill Cemetary Road became temporarily impassable due to water flowing over it.
Flooding was reported on several downtown streets in the city of Fayette.
Water was flowing over AL-86 in several spots, both west and east of the city of Pickensville.  Several roads in the city of Carrollton also had to be closed due to flooding.
A portion of AL-48 near the state line had to be closed due to a partially blocked culvert causing rain water to run over the road.
Several roads near the town of Millerville had to be closed due to flooding.
Water was running over the roadway near the intersection of AL-17 and Panola Parkway.  A home in the Geiger community was flooded.
Several locations in northern Greene County became flooded, including CR-60 near the Mantua community.  Several homes in the Jena community were also flooded.
Hidden Valley Road, near Steiner Lake, was temporarily impassable and had to be closed due to high water.
A portion of Romulus Road, near Jacobs Lane in the southwest corner of Tuscaloosa County, had to be closed due to flooding.
Several secondary roads west of Vernon, near AL-18, had to be closed due to flooding.
Numerous roads in the city of Moundville had to be closed due to flooding, and water entered and damaged several homes in the area.
A portion of AL-219 in Centreville had to be closed due to water flowing over it.

Several county roads around Chilton County became impassable due to flooding.  The hardest hit was CR-61, in the Jumbo community, where floodwater and associated debris caused several large sections of the paved road to wash out.
Many streets in downtown Columbiana became flooded.  The police department had to direct traffic around the flooded intersection of Main Street and Meyer Street.
Six to eight inches of water was flowing across AL-70, near the Dargin Crossroads community, north of Calera.
Several roads west of the city of Vernon had to be closed due to flooding.
Several trees were blown down in the Buhl community.
Several roads in downtown Vernon became temporarily impassable due to flooding.
Several roads in the city of Parrish had to be closed due to flooding.
Several roads in the city of Cordova had to be closed due to flooding.

A large oak tree was blown down onto a house on South 5th Street, in the city of Gadsden.  Saturated ground from recent rains likely contributed to the trees failure.  The fallen tree crushed the kitchen and another utility area of the house, causing considerable damage.

Several businesses and other buildings along Main Street in the city of Brent sustained significant water damage after a storm drain failed to keep up with flooding rains.  The buildings included a building supply company, a services building for the elderly, and a church.

More the two dozen people in and around the city of Brent had to be rescued from homes and trailers in the middle of the night, after storm drains became overwhelmed by heavy rain.  A section of Deer Creek Road, near Centreville, became washed out due to the rushing waters, and at least two vehicles subsequently drove into the newly formed ditch.
Several trees were blown down near the intersection of AL-28 and CR-57, in the Jefferson community.
Several trees were blown down on River Road, in the northern part of the county.
Winds estimated around 45 mph blew the tin roofing off of a building, on AL-17 in Vernon.
Trees were blown down at several locations near the Lamar County Airport.
Two trees were blown down on CR-35, near Carrollton.
Powerlines were blown down on AL-17, and 3rd Avenue, in the city of Aliceville.
Trees were blown down on AL-17, south of Kennedy.
Thunderstorm winds caused damage described as significant to several buildings in downtown Winfield.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in the Lynn community.
Trees and power lines were blown down on Scenic Drive, near Double Springs.
Several power lines were blown down in the city of Tuscaloosa.

A total of 20 to 30 large diameter hardwood trees were uprooted across several locations around the Empire community.  One home sustained damage from the fallen trees, and 4 outbuildings were also damaged.  A manufactured home had its roof peeled off.  Winds were estimated at 70 to 80 mph.
Several trees were blown down in the Arkadelphia community.
Trees and power lines were blown down near the intersection of US-31 and CR-7, in the Blount Springs community.
A power line was blown down across AL-160, just east of I-65.
Two trees were blown down near the Hortons Mill community, north of Oneonta.
A tree was blown down onto a power line on Kent Road, near the Susan Moore community.
Several trees and power lines were blown, and 3 houses were damaged, near Clanton Street in Attalla.
Numerous roads had to be closed due to flash flooding, across the western and central sections of Lamar County.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in the city of Attalla, with one tree falling onto and damaging a house.
Vandergrift Road, near the Midfield Park Shopping Center, became temporarily impassable due to flooding.  Several other roads in the area, including B.Y. Williams Drive, also became flooded.
A carport was displaced from a home at the intersection of US-431 and CR-65, in the Rock Stand community.
Another round of heavy rain caused the closure of several roads, in and around the city of Vernon.
Yet another round of heavy rain caused the closure of at least 7 more roads in Lamar County.
Several roads around the city of Gadsden had to be closed due to becoming temporarily impassable due to flooding.

The tornado touched down just south of the intersection of CR-19 and AL-129, near the community of Thorn Hill.  From there, it traveled northeast a little over two miles, over mostly wooded terrain, and lifted as it crossed AL-129.  Along the path, the tornado damaged the roofs of 4 homes, damaged 2 barns and one utility building, uprooted 20 hardwood trees, and snapped another 5 in half, and damaged several cars.

The effects of what was once Hurricane Ida, but had weakened into a Tropical Depression, were felt as early as Monday afternoon, November 9, in Pike, Barbour and Montgomery Counties, as light rain began falling around 2 pm.  The rain continued to move northward and intensified Monday night and into the day on Tuesday, November 10. Rains continued across Central Alabama through Tuesday evening.  By the time the last area of rain exited Cherokee and Cleburne Counties after midnight on Wednesday, November 11, nearly everyone across Central Alabama had seen at least 3 inches of rain.  The highest storm total rainfall of 9.83 inches was reported just south of Opelika.  Daily rainfall records were set on November 11 at Anniston (3.51 inches), Birmingham (4.01 inches), Montgomery (2.33 inches), and Tuscaloosa (2.89 inches).||Sustained winds around Central Alabama maxed out between 20 and 30 mph, with peak wind gusts generally between 30 and 40 mph. These winds blew down a few trees around the area, especially shallow rooted trees where the saturated soil likely played a significant role.
Heavy rain associated with the remnants of Tropical Depression Ida flooded several roads in the Mount Willing community.  Flood waters also entered 3 mobile homes, requiring evacuation.
Heavy rainfall from the remnants of Tropical Storm Ida caused several county roads across Lee County to become temporarily closed.
Heavy rain associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Ida caused several roads to become flooded in and around the city of Gadsden, leading to their temporary closure.
Heavy rainfall associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Ida caused a portion of Childersburg-Fayetteville Highway to become flooded and temporarily closed.

Heavy rainfall associated with the remnants of Tropical Storm Ida caused several roads around the cities of Anniston and Saks to become flooded and were temporarily closed. A 3 block area in downtown Anniston was, at one point, under 2.5 feet of water.

The highest storm total rainfall of 9.83 inches was reported just south of Opelika. Two trees were blown down on Bachelors Chapel Road, in the Hokes Bluff area.

Several roads in the city of Vernon had to be closed due to flooding, including AL-17 and AL-18.  Water eventually reached car hood level on a portion of AL-17. An apartment complex on AL-18 became flooded.
Several trees were blown down on roads just north of Lake Lurleen State Park.
Trees and power lines were blown down on Sipsey Valley Road.
Trees were blown down on Forest Road, in Hueytown.
A few trees were blown down in and around the city of Berry.

Numerous county, state, and US highways became flooded across Marion County, including CR-61, US-43, CR-11, US-78, and CR-52. Taylor Road in the city of Guin, and Providence Street in the city of Winfield, were also flooded.
A couple of trees were blown down on Pine Mountain Road, near the Remlap community.
A few trees and power lines were blown down in and around the city of Eutaw.
A couple of trees and power lines were blown down in the Shady Grove community.
Several trees were blown down in and around the city the Greensboro. One tree landed on a home and briefly trapped the occupant inside. No injuries were reported.
Several trees were blown down near exit 219 on Interstate 65, near Jemison, including some that were blown onto the highway.
A wind gust of 75 mph was measured by unknown measuring equipment near Maplesville.
A couple of trees and power lines were blown down on Temple Road, in the city of Clanton.
A few trees were blown down near the Clay/Coosa county line.
Two trees were blown down near the intersection of CR-129 and AL-48, near Wedowee.
Several trees were blown down in the southeastern part of Randolph County.
Strong gradient winds blew down isolated trees at several locations around the Birmingham metro area.
Strong gradient winds caused a gas station awning to tip over, on  Blue Mountain Road in Anniston.
Power lines were blown down on 4th Street, in Pleasant Grove.
Street flooding was reported on Magnolia Street, in Childersburg.
Street flooding was reported on Betsy Ross lane, in Sylacauga.
An estimated 3 to 4 inches of rain in a short time lead to flash flooding of several roads in the southeastern portion of Bullock County, some of which became impassable due to the high water.
An estimated 6 inches of rain in a short time caused several dirt roads to become washed out near the Pittsview community.
Repeated heavy rainfall led to the closure of a portion of CR-318, due to water flowing over a bridge.
A portion of AL-95 south of Eufaula had to be closed for a short time due to flash flooding.
A prolonged period of rain caused a portion of AL-70 to become impassable due to high water, in the city of Columbiana.
A prolonged period of rainfall caused a portion of Alabama Avenue to become flooded, in the city of Sylacauga.
Several inches of water was flowing across a portion of AL-18, in the city of Vernon.
A Christmas tree in front of the Tuscaloosa County Courthouse was blown down.  Numerous trees were blown down near the Jim Walters Resources number 7 mine.
A portion of Cotton Hill Road, near the intersection with AL-30, became partially washed out due to water flowing over it.

A period of snow followed by dropping temperatures led to numerous slick roads across Blount County. Roads around the communities of Locust Fork, Hayden, and Snead, as well as the city of Oneonta, had to be closed due to ice formation on them. The icy roads lasted into the overnight hours, long after the precipitation had quit falling.
Numerous roads across Etowah County became icy, and driving on them was described as treacherous, due to a period of snow that fell when temperatures were close to 32 degrees.
A portion of AL-68, near the Cherokee/Dekalb County line, became icy and very hazardous to travel on.
Several large trees were blown down south of Roanoke.
A spotter with a hand held anemometer measured winds up to 70 mph near the Peach Park exit, at Interstate 65 and US-31 near Clanton.
Several trees and power lines were blown down.
Rainfall of 5.3 inches in a short time caused water to enter at least one house and flood it up to 2 inches.
Widespread flooding was reported around the city of Wedowee, and several roads had to be closed for several hours due to high water.
Several trees and large tree limbs were blown down around the cities of Valley and Lanett.

As many as 6 roads in and around the city of Ohatchee were closed due to water flowing over them.  Rock Springs had 2 to 3 feet of flowing water, and Horse Bend Road had 1 to 1.5 feet of flowing water.
Winds estimated around 45 mph caused a portion of a roof of a mobile home to be blown off, near the Collins Chapel community.
In the Buffalo community, the equipment barn of a farm had its metal roof blown off and scattered into an adjacent pasture.  Winds were estimated around 45 mph.
A period of snow accumulated to between 1 and 2 inches across Greene County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to between 1 and 2 inches across Hale County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to between 1 and 2 inches across Tuscaloosa County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to between 1 and 1.5 inches across Perry County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to around 1 inch across Bibb County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of around 2 inches across Chilton County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
Despite snow falling for several hours, accumulations across Russell County averaged just around 2 inches. The snow did cause hazardous travel conditions for a period of time.

Although there were isolated unconfirmed reports of up to 4 inches of snow in the northeastern part of Jefferson County, average accumulations around the county were generally 2 inches or less. The snow did cause a period of hazardous travel, especially on the multiple interstate highways that pass through the metropolitan area. This caused  Birmingham area police to temporarily block interstate on-ramps around the city.

Although there were isolated reports of up to 2.5 inches of snow on Oak Mountain, average accumulations around the county were generally between 1 and 2 inches. The snow did cause a period of hazardous travel, especially on the interstate and major US highways that pass through the county.

Although there were isolated reports of up to 3 inches of snow in the higher elevations along the southern county line, average accumulations around the county were generally between 1 and 2 inches. The snow did cause a period of hazardous travel, which resulted in several accidents.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of 1 to 2 inches across Talladega county, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of around 2 inches across St. Clair County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of 1.5 to 2 inches across Etowah County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of around 2 inches across Calhoun County, causing hazardous travel conditions.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of around 1.5 inches across Clay County, causing hazardous travel conditions.

An average of 2 to 4 inches of snow fell across Sumter County, especially in the southern half of the county in the Bellamy, Ward, and Cuba communities. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.

An average of 2 to 4 inches of snow fell across Marengo County, especially in the southern half of the county in the Dixons Mill community. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.

An average of 2 to 2.5 inches of snow fell across Dallas County, especially in the southern half of the county in the Southside community, southeast of Selma. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.

An average of 2 to 3.5 inches of snow fell across Autauga County, especially in the southern half of the county around the city of Prattville. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
An average of 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the whole of Lowndes County. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
An average of 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the whole of Tallapoosa County. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.

An average of 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the whole of Montgomery County. The highest amount, 4 inches, was observed in the Ramer community.  Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.  On AL-110, near the Pike Road community, a vehicle lost control and slid into a pond, killing a 4-year-old and a 2-year-old passenger (both indirect), and injuring (indirect) the mother that was driving.

A several hour period of moderate to heavy snow led to significant accumulations across Pike County.  Snowfall totals averaged between 3 and 5 inches. The highest amount, 7 inches, was reported around Troy.  Many roads, especially bridges and other elevated surfaces, became icy and hazardous.  Most county roads had to be closed for a period of time.

A several hour period of moderate to heavy snow led to significant accumulations across Barbour County.  Snowfall totals averaged around 4 inches. The highest amount, 5 inches, was reported in the Clio community.  Many roads, especially bridges and other elevated surfaces, became icy and hazardous.  Most county roads had to be closed for a period of time.

A period of moderate to heavy snow led to significant accumulations across Bullock County.  Snowfall totals averaged 3 to 4 inches.   Many roads, especially bridges and other elevated surfaces, became icy and hazardous, and several traffic accidents were reported.

A period of moderate to heavy snow led to significant accumulations across Macon County.  Snowfall totals averaged 3 to 4 inches.   Many roads, especially bridges and other elevated surfaces, became icy and hazardous.

A period of moderate to heavy snow led to significant accumulations across Lee County.  Snowfall totals averaged 3 to 4 inches.  Many roads, especially bridges and other elevated surfaces, became icy and hazardous.
An average of 2 to 2.5 inches of snow fell across the whole of Chambers County. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.

An average of 2.5 to 3.5 inches of snow fell across the whole of Randolph County. The highest amount, just under 4 inches, was reported in the Rock Stand community. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
An average of 3 to 4 inches of snow fell across the whole of Cleburne County.  Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
An average of 2 to 3 inches of snow fell across the whole of Cherokee County.  Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
A period of snow accumulated to an average of around 2 inches across Coosa County, causing hazardous travel conditions.

An average of 2 to 3.5 inches of snow fell across Elmore County, especially in the southern half of the county around the city of Wetumpka. Many bridges and other elevated surfaces became icy and hazardous.
Lightning was the suspected cause of a house fire on Locksley Road, in Mountain Brook. The fire destroyed the home's roof, and caused considerable damage to the attic and other areas of the home.

The tornado touched down just northwest of the city limits of Clanton, near the intersection of CR-406 and CR-53.  From there it moved east-northeast into the northern part of the city, and lifted just after crossing US-31 west of the hospital. At least five structures received damage, with much of it consisting of shingles being blown off.  One garage and a gazebo were heavily damaged, and one large storage building was totally destroyed with debris scattered nearly 1 1/2 miles downstream.  Eight to 10 hardwood trees were uprooted and 6 to 9 smaller hard and soft wood trees were snapped.

The tornado first touched down on Fox Valley Road in the Maylene community, where it tossed trampolines and snapped at few small trees. It then traveled northeast, crossing CR-17 just south of the intersection of 1st Ave W. It then struck Fox Valley Apartments and moved into the Stoney Meadow Subdivision, where several homes received minor to substantial roof damage. The most significant damage occurred on Rock View Trail, where siding was stripped off of one home and another home received significant roof damage and had the garage door blown out. Two mature cedar trees were also snapped at this location. The tornado weakened rapidly and continued to produce minor damage as it crossed through the Navajo Trail Subdivision. The last bits of minor roof and fence damage were in the Greenfield Subdivision off of Industrial Park Drive in Alabaster.  In total, at least 20 structures were damaged, and dozens of trees were snapped or uprooted.
An average of 1 to 2 inches of snow fell across Blount county.  Several roads in the county, especially near the Susan Moore community, briefly became impassible due to slightly higher accumulations.

An average of 1 to 2 inches of snow fell across Etowah County, although isolated heavier amounts were reported in some higher elevations.  This caused several roads around the county to become quite slippery and hazardous to travel.

An average of 1 to 2 inches of snow fell across Cherokee County, although isolated heavier amounts were reported in some higher elevations.  This caused several roads around the county to become quite slippery and hazardous to travel.
Several trees were blown down on the 3800 block of Steele Street, and the windows were blown out of a building on Military Street, both on the southern side of Hamilton.
Hail ranging from golf ball to tennis ball sized fell in a swath from Carbon Hill to the Lupton community.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in the city of Clanton, resulting in power outages.
A wind gust of 70 mph was measured at the EOC in downtown Hamilton.
Two houses and one mobile home sustained roof damage, 2 barns were damaged, and several more trees were blown down, near Black Oak Church, on CR-57.

What began as flash flooding transitioned into widespread long term flooding across a large portion of Shelby County during the late morning of the 10th.  Dozens of roads were closed across the county due to high water, and as many as ten roads were still closed two days later. The hardest hit area was the western portion of the county, especially around the Helena, Pelham, and Alabaster areas, where more than 8 inches of rain fell during the 3 day period.  In Alabaster, several vehicles were overcome by high water, and the occupants briefly became trapped.  Other communities that experienced flooding included Montevallo, Columbiana, Shelby, and Wilsonville.

What began as flash flooding transitioned into widespread long term flooding across a large portion of Talladega County during the late morning of the 10th.  Dozens of roads were closed across the county due to high water, and several small bridges became washed out.  The initial problem area on the morning of the 10th was the city of Sylacauga, but as the heavy rainfall shifted northward in the afternoon, the cities of Talladega and eventually Munford also experienced flooding issues.  Other communities with reports of flooding included Childersburg, Winterboro, and Renfroe.

A period of heavy rain caused Bishop Creek to come out of its banks, and the water came up to the bottom of a few vehicles in the area.  Flash flooding in the area later transitioned to long term areal flooding due to additional rainfall.
Six inches of water was flowing over McGowans Ferry Road near the Fayetteville community.
After briefly letting up for a short time, another burst of heavy rainfall caused flash flooding in the city of Pelham.  Several people had to be rescued from flooded townhomes.
One foot of water was reported flowing over Deaver Walker Road, near the Locust Fork community.

The short-lived tornado touched down on the northernmost ball field in Blountsville Park, where it ripped the tin roofing off the dugouts and carried them to a tree line approximately 300 to 400 yards down the path.  It then continued to the north-northeast for less than a quater mile and crossed Park Drive, where it damaged a portion of the roof of a house.  One large oak tree with a poor root system was also uprooted.

Numerous trees were blown down in a swath from Attalla to the north side of Gadsden.  Some trees were blown down and blocked a portion of Interstate 59, north of exit 183, and both lanes of the highway had to be closed for a short time to clear them.

Several trees were blown down near the intersection of Patterson Street and Alexander Drive, near the Sardis City community.  A portion of a garage roof was blown off, and a home sustained damage from a fallen tree.
A house fire, with unspecified damages, was caused by a lightning strike in the New Union community.

A house sustained significant damage from fire after being struck by lightning, in the Altadena Bend neighborhood near the Jefferson and Shelby County line.  The residents heard the loud boom of thunder, and then had only a few minutes to get out of the house before it became engulfed.  The fire destroyed the attic and upper floor of the two-story home.  Three firefighters were injured (indirect) when the back deck on which they were standing collapsed, as they were dousing hot spots.
Several trees were blown down in the city of Aliceville.
A tree fell onto and damaged a car and a business building on AL-18, in the Bankston community.

A swath of wind damage cut across the southern half of Sumter County, from west of the Ward community, east-northeastward to south of Bellamy.  Dozens of trees were snapped and uprooted, many of them blocking roads.  One home near CR-10 southeast of Ward received minor roof damage.  The driver of a vehicle became trapped by fallen trees near AL-17.
A brief tornado touchdown, producing no observable damage, was reported by Fire Department personnel in the Ward community.
Several trees and power lines were blown down in and around the city of Demopolis.
Two power poles were snapped off, about 2 miles north of the intersection of US-80 and AL-69, in the southern part of Hale County.

The tornado first touched down about 5 miles northeast of Greensboro, near the intersection of AL-25 and Crawford Road.  It then tracked northeastward, roughly parallel to AL-25, for nearly 6 miles, and lifted just north of Starling Road. Three homes sustained minor damage, one barn was destroyed, and metal sheeting was torn off an outbuilding.  At least 40 trees were uprooted along the path, some of them blocking portions of AL-25.
Several trees were blown down onto US-278, between Sulligent and Beaverton, and blocked all 4 lanes of traffic.
Several trees were blown down in the Pebble community.
Trees were blown down onto a power line on Indian Mound Road, southeast of Hamilton.

The tornado touched down on US-43 just south of the Gu-Win community.  From there it produced a sporadic damage path to the northeast for a little over 7 miles, crossing AL-253, CR-61, US-78, and AL-129, before lifting on the southwest side of Brilliant.  Three homes took the brunt of the damage, all located southwest of Brilliant along County Road 47. One home had minor damage due to fallen trees. One of these trees uprooted and flipped a minivan upside down. The second home had minor roof damage and two outbuildings on the property that were destroyed. The third home incurred major structural damage when the windward side of the garage was blown in. There was also an outbuilding that flipped over at the third home location. In total, 40 to 60 hardwood trees were uprooted along the path.
Trees were blown down on CR-46, northeast of Brilliant.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of CR-15 and Fulmer Road, just west of US-43.  It then tracked northeastward for about 6.5 miles, crossing US-43 and CR-63 on the southern city limits of Berry.  Four homes on CR-56 southwest of Berry received minor damage, ranging from shingle damage to garage door blown in.  One metal outbuilding was destroyed.  Around 50 trees were snapped or uprooted along the path.

The tornado touched down in southeastern Fayette County about 4 miles northeast of Berry.  It then tracked northeastward through mostly a wooded rural area, before crossing into Walker County.  In Fayette County, damage was mainly confined to about 2 dozen trees that were snapped and uprooted.

The tornado first touched down about 4 miles northeast of Brooksville, and then tracked northeastward. It was on the ground for less than a mile before moving across the county line into Marshall County, just west of the intersection of Panky Lane and Nixon Chapel Road. Within Blount County, two structures were damaged and hundreds of trees were snapped and uprooted.  One mobile home was moved off its foundation and also damaged by fallen trees.

Trees and power lines were blown down northwest of Gallant and east of Altoona.  One 32 year old man was killed (indirect) when the car he was a passenger in struck a tree that had fallen across the road.
Winds estimated around 80 mph uprooted 5 hardwood trees, damaged the roof of a house, and damaged a travel trailer.  All this occurred on CR-9, southwest of West Blocton.
Trees were blown down onto power lines on Troy Road, east of Hokes Bluff.
Trees were blown down at several locations around the city of Centre.

The tornado touched down at the City Landing area of Demopolis, and from there moved on a north-northeast path.  At City Landing, at least 20 people witnessed the tornado and ran for shelter. At least 20 vehicles were damaged, many with windows blown out. Tool boxes were ripped off the back of a few trucks and were thrown into other vehicles, and many trees were snapped off in the area.  The tornado then crossed US-43 and moved into a rural part of the county, before crossing the Black Warrior River and moving into Greene County.

The tornado that had touched down in Marengo County, near the city of Demopolis, moved into Greene County.  On its northeast path, it produced sporadic tree damage, and stayed mostly in forested areas. Just before crossing the Black Warrior River for the second time, it struck the Greene County Steam Plant, where 2 men were injured when they were blown down by the wind.  A few small buildings were damaged in the same area, and a tractor trailer rig was blown over and moved at least 40 feet.  The tornado then moved into Hale County.

After touching down in Marengo County, and moving across a portion of Greene County, the Demopolis Tornado crossed the Black Warrior River for a second time and moved into Hale County.  Within Hale County, the tornado stayed over primarily wooded terrain, and caused sporadic tree damage.

The tornado that first touched down near Berry, in Fayette County, moved into Walker County near where AL-18 crosses Frost Creek.  From there it continued its northeast path, and eventually lifted about 5 miles west of Oakman.  In Walker County, the tornado blew down a 100 foot radio tower and damaged an adjoining shed.  Numerous trees were also snapped or uprooted.

This long tracked, strong, tornado first touched down in the Walker County city of Parrish.  It then remained on the ground for 54 minutes, traversing nearly 30 miles in three counties.  The vast majority of the damage was done in Walker County.  In addition to Parrish, heavy damaged occurred in the cities of Cordova, Sumiton, and Empire.  Between 70 and 80 homes and other buildings along the path received varying degrees of damage, and at least one home in Parrish was completely destroyed. Somewhere between 800 and 1000 trees were snapped, with a similar number uprooted.  While there were no known deaths or injuries directly caused by the tornado, one 50 year old woman died (indirect) after she slipped and fell while going to a storm shelter.  The tornado moved into Jefferson County near the intersection of Bankston Road and County Line Road.

After crossing into Jefferson County from Walker County, the Parrish Tornado continued its northeastward path.  Damage in Jefferson County primarily consisted of trees that were blown down and snapped.  A tree fell into and broke a living room window of a home on Arkadelphia Road, and a large storage shed had its roof torn off.

After crossing into Blount County from Jefferson County, the Parrish Tornado crossed Interstate 65 near exit 284, and finally lifted southwest of the Hayden community, between the Interstate and McCay Lake.  As in Jefferson County, the damage in Blount County primarily consisted of trees that were blown down and snapped.

The tornado touched down near the intersection of Winston CR 28 and AL Hwy 13 at approximately 205 am, then traveled northeast across CR 13 towards Macedonia. The tornado reached its maximum strength wind speeds of 100 to 110 mph as it crossed CR 3231. The width of the damage path at this point was approx 600 yards, the widest portion of the damage path. The tornado then crossed CR 3230 where it destroyed a two week old hay barn and a large workshop/storage shed and also caused significant damage to two other structures.||Another outbuilding also sustained damage at the same location and the residence sustained significant roof damage. At this point the damage path took more of an easterly path but remained narrow and well-defined. The tornado struck just north of the Macedonia church  where a double-wide home sustained significant roof damage and several outbuildings were damaged. It continued eastward just north of Friendship Rd and then crossed AL Hwy 195 as it continued to snap off large tree limbs and caused damage to additional outbuildings. The last damage found was near the intersection of CR 2 and CR 47, where minor roof damage affected a home and tree damage was present. The tornado then moved off into inaccessible forestry land and dissipated.

The tornado initially touched down approximately 3.5 miles northeast of the Birmingham airport near L.M. Smith Middle School and traveled northeast crossing Huffman Road, Center Point Parkway, Old Springville Road and Brewster Road. The tornado dissipated just south of the Grayson Valley Country Club. The tornado touched down about 1 mile southwest of the city of Millport, where it uprooted several trees.  From there, it moved northeastward and crossed AL-17 about a half mile west of Millport. On both sides of the highway, 50 to 70 trees were either snapped off or uprooted, and a few homes sustained shingle damage. Tree limbs were actually embedded into the roof of one home. In the same general area, a tractor trailer was overturned and a metal roof was blown off a garage building. In addition, Metal roof stripping was blown off a barn roof and was transported 100 yards downstream into the top of a 60 foot tree. The tornado lifted on the north side of Millport, near James Street, where a few more trees were snapped off and a barn was damaged.
Several locations in western Lamar County became covered with water and temporarily impassable, including Old Calvert Road, Easlon Branch Road, and Millie.

From there, the tornado traveled eastward and crossed Black Road, where a metal car port had its roof pulled off.  Another home had a portion of its roof removed and a large section of privacy fence was toppled. The tornado then traveled along CR-6 for about a mile, crossing CR-49. The most significant damage was near the intersection of County Roads 49 and 6, where several large hardwood trees were uprooted.  The tornado lifted just east of Wilson Road, where a metal building suffered damage.

The tornado touched down near the Selma Highway and CR-29, just south of the Autauga County Airport, where a few trees were snapped off. A quasi linear convective system produced an EF1 tornado, with winds estimated at 100 mph, in the city of Vestavia Hills. The path was 0.4 miles long and 100 yards wide. The brief tornado touched down near the Vestavia Hills Police Department along Highway 31, traveled northeast crossing Bird Park and lifted just to the north of the Vestavia Hills Country Club, near Glenwood Road. Numerous hardwood trees were uprooted and thirty pine trees in Bird Park were snapped. An automobile sustained damage when its windows were blown out. Several buildings, homes and fencing were damaged; most due to fallen trees. One home sustained significant damage as the drywall fasteners on the ceiling were loosened by the force of the winds.

To the south of a brief EF1 tornado path in Vestavia Hills, strong rear inflow notch winds up to 90 mph snapped or uprooted dozens of hardwood and softwood trees, some causing damage to homes as they fell.  This damage began near Old Creek Trail, just west of Highway 31, crossed Highway 31 just north of Georgia Ave, and continued east across the southern portion of Vestavia Hills Country Club.
